meta.titre: Current electricity: charge, current, potential difference and resistance
meta.sous_theme: Charge, current, potential difference, resistance and AC

sections.contenu_markdown: When a trader in Douala charges a phone with a power bank during a power cut, charge flows from the battery through a cable and energy stored in the battery is transferred to the phone. Every electrical question in the GCE starts from the same ideas: charge, current, potential difference and resistance. You must know their units, the instruments that measure them, and how to link them with simple formulae. The same questions also test the difference between direct current from a battery and alternating current from the mains.

items: Metals contain free electrons that can move through the whole conductor.
A cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
Energy is measured in joules, time in seconds, and one minute is 60 seconds.

sections.titre: Charge, current, potential difference and resistance
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Electric current** is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit:

$$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$

with $Q$ in coulombs (C), $t$ in seconds (s) and $I$ in amperes (A). One ampere is one coulomb per second. In a metal the charge carriers are electrons, which move from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. By convention, the **conventional current** is drawn in the opposite direction, from positive to negative.

**Potential difference** (p.d.) between two points is the energy changed from electrical form to other forms per coulomb of charge passing between them:

$$V = \frac{W}{Q}$$

One volt is one joule per coulomb. The **e.m.f.** of a source is the energy it supplies per coulomb of charge that passes through it (the whole circuit).

**Resistance** is the opposition of a conductor to the flow of charge: $R = V/I$ (unit: ohm). For a wire, $R$ rises with its length and falls when its cross-sectional area increases; it also depends on the material and the temperature.

| Quantity | Unit | Instrument | Connection |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current | ampere (A) | ammeter | in series |
| Potential difference | volt (V) | voltmeter | in parallel |
| Charge | coulomb (C) | calculated from $Q = It$ | not applicable |

Electrical energy and power follow from the definitions: $W = QV = IVt$ and $P = IV$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a circuit diagram description asks where to place the ammeter or the voltmeter
variantes.contenu_markdown: An ammeter has a very low resistance, so it is connected in series: the whole current in that branch passes through it. A voltmeter has a very high resistance, so it is connected in parallel across the component being measured; it takes almost no current. Current is the same everywhere in a series loop. It is never used up: the charge returns to the cell, and only the energy of the charge is transferred to the components.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when you must distinguish e.m.f. from p.d. or calculate the energy supplied
variantes.contenu_markdown: The e.m.f. is the energy given to each coulomb by the cell or the generator. The p.d. across a lamp is the energy that each coulomb gives to the lamp. For a lamp working with a steady current, the energy transferred is $W = QV$. If a cell has an e.m.f. of $1.5\,\mathrm{V}$, it gives $1.5\,\mathrm{J}$ to every coulomb that goes through it.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked to compare a battery with the mains or to explain the use of AC for transmission
variantes.contenu_markdown: A direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only; batteries and solar cells give d.c. An alternating current (a.c.) reverses its direction regularly; the mains in Cameroon is about $220\,\mathrm{V}$ with a frequency of $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (50 complete cycles each second). A.c. is preferred for transmission of power because its voltage can be raised or lowered with a transformer. Power is sent at a high voltage and low current, which reduces the energy wasted as heat in the cables, then it is reduced to a safe value near the homes.

sections.enonce_markdown: A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ battery sends a steady current through a lamp. The charge that passes through the lamp in $3$ minutes is $90\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculate (a) the current in the lamp, (b) the electrical energy transferred to the lamp in this time, and (c) the power of the lamp. Check (c) by a second method.

etapes.justification: The coulomb and the ampere are defined with time in seconds.
Current is charge divided by time, $I = Q/t$.
From $V = W/Q$ the energy is $W = QV$.
Power is energy divided by time.
A second method must give the same result.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The lamp carries $0.50\,\mathrm{A}$, receives $1080\,\mathrm{J}$ in 3 minutes and has a power of $6.0\,\mathrm{W}$. Both methods agree.

items.erreur_markdown: The ammeter is connected in parallel across the lamp to measure the current.
items.pourquoi_faux: An ammeter has a very low resistance. In parallel it would let a very large current flow through it, which can damage it and short-circuit the lamp.
items.correction_markdown: Connect the ammeter in series, and the voltmeter in parallel.

items.erreur_markdown: Current is used up as it passes through a lamp, so the current is smaller after the lamp.
items.pourquoi_faux: In a series circuit the current is the same at every point. Charge is not destroyed. What is transferred to the lamp is the energy of the charge.
items.correction_markdown: Current is the same before and after the lamp; the potential energy of each coulomb is smaller after it.

items.erreur_markdown: In a wire, conventional current and electron flow are in the same direction.
items.pourquoi_faux: Electrons are negative, so they move from the negative to the positive terminal. Conventional current is defined as the flow of positive charge, from positive to negative.
items.correction_markdown: Draw the conventional current from + to − outside the cell, and say that electrons drift in the opposite direction.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the time in minutes in $Q = It$: $0.4\,\mathrm{A} \times 2 = 0.8\,\mathrm{C}$ for 2 minutes.
items.pourquoi_faux: The time must be in seconds. $2$ minutes is $120\,\mathrm{s}$, so the charge is $0.4 \times 120 = 48\,\mathrm{C}$.
items.correction_markdown: Convert minutes to seconds (and hours to seconds) before using $Q = It$.

items.erreur_markdown: Alternating current is preferred because it flows faster than direct current.
items.pourquoi_faux: The reason is not speed. A.c. voltage can be stepped up and down by transformers, and high-voltage transmission reduces the energy lost as heat in the cables.
items.correction_markdown: Say that a.c. can be transformed, so power is transmitted at high voltage and low current with little loss.

items.enonce_markdown: A steady current of $2.5\,\mathrm{A}$ flows in a wire for $40\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the charge that passes through the wire.

A small motor draws a current of $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$ from a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ battery for $5$ minutes. Calculate (a) the charge that passes through the motor, and (b) the electrical energy supplied to the motor.

A $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ battery supplies a steady current of $0.50\,\mathrm{A}$ to a radio for $40$ hours before it is exhausted. Calculate (a) the total charge that passes through the radio, (b) the total electrical energy delivered, and (c) the power of the radio.

items_markdown: **Current** $I = Q/t$ (ampere = coulomb per second). Conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to the electron flow.
**Potential difference** $V = W/Q$ (volt = joule per coulomb); **resistance** $R = V/I$ (ohm).
Ammeter in **series**, voltmeter in **parallel**. Current is the same at all points of a series loop and is never used up.
Energy and power: $W = QV = IVt$ and $P = IV$. Convert minutes and hours to seconds.
**A.c.** can be stepped up and down by transformers, so electrical power is transmitted at high voltage and low current with less energy lost in the cables.
